result.title: Dry-season malaria transmission and associated risk factors among urban residents of Jabi Tehnan District, northwest Ethiopia
result.authorString: Yeshanew S, Kendie FA, Atenafu G, Nibret E.
result.abstractText: Background Dry-season malaria transmission is a growing public health challenge in urban areas of Ethiopia. However, concrete evidence on its magnitude and associated factors remains scarce. The present study, therefore, assessed the extent of malaria transmission and identified factors associated with malaria among urban residents of Jabi Tehnan District during the dry season. Methods A community-based cross-sectional study was conducted in March 2026 among 335 residents of Finote Selam, Mankusa, and Jiga towns. One eligible adult from each selected household was tested for malaria using a CareStart™ Malaria Pf/Pv Ag Combo rapid diagnostic test (RDT). Sociodemographic and malaria-related data were collected using a pretested structured questionnaire. Associations were assessed using multivariable logistic regression and reported as adjusted odds ratios (AORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Statistical significance was considered at p < 0.05. Results Malaria prevalence was 17.6% (59/335), with cases detected in all urban centers of the district. Plasmodium falciparum was the predominant parasite identified (59.3%), while mixed P. falciparum/P. vivax infections accounted for 6.8% of cases. Individuals engaged in farming activities (AOR=3.575; 95% CI: 1.218-8.858), houses with eave openings (AOR=9.635; 95% CI: 2.718-34.155), and inadequate knowledge about malaria preventive measures (AOR=2.218; 95% CI: 1.011-5.301) appeared as significant explanatory risk factors associated with increased odds of malaria. In contrast, insecticide-treated nets (ITNs) utilization was associated with reduced odds of infection (AOR=0.076; 95% CI: 0.011-0.525). Conclusion Dry-season malaria transmission persists among urban residents of Jabi Tehnan District. Strengthening personal protection during farming activities and ITNs utilization at home, improving housing conditions, and promoting malaria-related health education should be prioritized alongside targeted surveillance and vector-control interventions.

result.title: Prevalence and factors contributing to malaria infection among the under five children attending Buvuma Health Centre IV in Buvuma Island District
result.abstractText: Background Malaria is the leading cause of morbidity and mortality among under-five children in Uganda especially in hard-to-reach areas such as islands. This study aimed at determining the prevalence and factors associated with malaria infection among under-five children attending Buvuma Health Centre-IV in Buvuma District. Methods Across-sectional study was conducted among the under-five children attending the facility, data was collected using a structured questionnaire and malaria diagnostic test results. Descriptive statistics were used to determine prevalence, and multivariate logistic regression was performed to identify factors independently contributing to malaria infection. Results Overall, 57.6% of the 243 participants tested positive for malaria. In this study, bivariate analysis was done on all variables that were seen necessary to cause or risk malaria infection. In Multivariate analysis, children whose caregivers incurred transport costs of UGX 11,000–15,000 (p = 0.020) and those living in households without window or door screening (p = 0.038) were significantly more likely to test positive for malaria. Children from middle-income households (UGX 210,000–400,000) were also more likely to have malaria (p = 0.042). Children aged 48-59months (p = 0.035) and those living in households with 3–4 rooms (p = 0.011) were less likely to test positive. Conclusion Malaria prevalence in Buvuma Island setting remains high. Structural housing characteristics, healthcare accessibility and social-economic factors were significantly associated with the infection. Strengthening household-level vector control, promoting early care-seeking and improving community malaria services may reduce the burden among under-five children.

result.title: Establishing a blood-stage controlled human malaria infection model with Plasmodium falciparum in healthy semi-immune Tanzanian adults
result.authorString: Silk SE, Salkeld J, Hassan O, Balige N, Mohamed L, Milando F, Barrett JR, Ahmed S, Kahatano A, Kessy E, Kweyamba P, Quinkert D, Juma O, Mwalimu B, Mohamed M, Marchevsky NG, Hofer LM, Mohamed M, Tarimo BB, Msami H, Mwamlima TG, Kalinga WF, Sasamalo IA, Mtaka IM, Lilolime NS, Donnellan FR, Bardelli M, Diouf A, Lawrie AM, Roberts R, Nugent FL, Long CA, Mswata S, Kasubi M, Cho J, Nielsen CM, Draper SJ, Minassian AM, Olotu AI.
result.abstractText: Controlled human malaria infection (CHMI) studies are a critical tool for the assessment and down-selection of potential malaria interventions, allowing detailed characterisation and understanding of host-parasite responses to inform both malaria vaccine and antimalarial drug development in humans. Blood-stage CHMI offers a specific means for proof-of-concept testing of blood-stage malaria vaccines, bypassing the pre-erythrocytic stages of malaria infection. Here, we establish a blood-stage CHMI model in an endemic region in a clinical study involving 12 healthy semi-immune male adult participants residing in Bagamoyo district, Tanzania. Participants were enrolled into relatively 'low' (n=6) and 'high' (n=6) malaria pre-exposure groups as defined by serum anti-schizont IgG levels. Participants were challenged with approximately 1000 erythrocytes infected with a chloroquine-sensitive Plasmodium falciparum 3D7 clone and closely monitored for 28 days at the Ifakara Health Institute clinical trial facility in Bagamoyo. Blood samples were collected for safety and immunology assessments, with venous blood samples for P. falciparum quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) taken once on day after challenge (C+1) and twice daily from two to 28 days after challenge (C+2 to C+28). Participants were treated once pre-defined diagnostic criteria were met or at day 28 (if criteria not met). The challenge inoculum was found to be safe with the severity grading of adverse events (AEs) in keeping with previous challenge studies. Overall, fewer AEs were reported as compared to malaria-naive UK adults previously challenged with the same inoculum dose, despite a 50-fold higher treatment threshold being used in Tanzanian adults. Nine of 11 participants developed parasitaemia detectable by qPCR and one participant was retrospectively excluded from parasitaemia endpoint analysis due to non-3D7 type infection. The two participants who remained qPCR negative were both in the 'high' pre-exposure group. Higher anti-schizont baseline serology status was associated with later median time to parasitaemia detection and time to pre-defined treatment criteria. These data demonstrate that blood-stage CHMI is safe and feasible in semi-immune adults in a malaria-endemic setting.

result.title: Culturally Grounded Malaria Knowledge among Traditional Health Practitioners and Elders in Rural Limpopo South Africa
result.abstractText: Community participation is central to malaria elimination, particularly in rural settings where Indigenous and biomedical health systems coexist. South African studies have documented household knowledge, attitudes and practices, but less is known about how traditional health practitioners and elders organise, communicate and apply malaria knowledge. Understanding these knowledge systems may strengthen culturally credible communication, timely referral and participation in elimination activities. This study explored culturally grounded knowledge of malaria symptoms, transmission, seasonal risk and prevention among traditional health practitioners and elders in Dan Village, Limpopo Province, and considered its implications for community engagement in malaria elimination. An exploratory qualitative design informed by Afrocentricity was used. Twenty-five participants - five diviners, five herbalists and fifteen elders aged 70 years or older - were purposively selected. Semi-structured interviews were conducted in Sepedi or Xitsonga, audio-recorded and transcribed. Thematic content analysis identified units of meaning, clustered related accounts and interpreted the resulting themes through cultural location, Nommo, Maat and Ubuntu. Participant accounts were distinguished from clinically or epidemiologically verified claims. Four themes were identified: recognition of malaria through symptom clusters; mosquito transmission within plural explanations of illness; seasonal ecological knowledge; and prevention as collective environmental responsibility. Participants linked fever, headache, chills, weakness and gastrointestinal symptoms with mosquito bites, rainfall, humidity, standing water and vegetation change. Their prevention accounts emphasised environmental management, reduced mosquito contact, community cooperation and early response to symptoms. Plant-based and spiritual practices were also reported but were not evaluated for safety or efficacy. The accounts showed areas of convergence with public-health guidance alongside claims requiring clarification or empirical assessment. Traditional practitioners and elders held context-specific knowledge that could support locally credible malaria communication, seasonal mobilisation and referral. Elimination programmes should engage trusted knowledge holders through structured, evidence-informed partnerships that preserve prompt parasitological diagnosis and recommended treatment while correcting unsafe or unverified claims.

result.title: Effects of a clinical decision support algorithm on malaria testing and treatment among febrile children in Tanzania: Findings from a mixed-methods cluster-randomized trial (DYNAMIC study)
result.authorString: Luwanda LB, Bohle LF, Taffé P, Kulinkina AV, Kavishe GA, Enos C, Mangu CD, Hassan F, Joram M, Miauton A, Mtebene I, Agrea P, Ashery GI, Masanja H, Ntinginya NE, D'Acremont V, Tan R.
result.abstractText: Background Effective malaria case management relies on consistent testing and appropriate treatment of febrile children. Yet adherence to these practices remains suboptimal in many endemic settings. Digital clinical decision support algorithms (CDSAs) such as ePOCT+ have been proposed to improve clinical guideline adherence. Methods This study presents a pre-specified secondary outcome analysis from the DYNAMIC cluster-randomized trial in Tanzania, evaluating the impact of the ePOCT+ CDSA on malaria case management (testing and treatment) among febrile children aged 2 months to 14 years in 40 primary health facilities. Quantitative data were analyzed using generalized linear mixed models, and where appropriate, Poisson regression models with a log link and robust standard errors. Qualitative interviews were conducted with healthcare providers in 15 purposively selected health facilities. Results Malaria testing was performed in 89.0% (8,931/10,037) of febrile children in the ePOCT + arm versus 71.9% (6,780/9,431) in routine care (adjusted risk ratio [aRR] 1.33; 95% Confidence Interval [CI]I 1.06–1.67). This effect was substantially larger in facilities with low malaria test positivity rates (< 5%; aRR 2.31, 95% CI 1.83–3.87) than in those with higher positivity rates (≥ 5%; aRR 1.09, 95% CI 1.03–1.15), suggesting ePOCT + may be particularly valuable where providers might otherwise deprioritize testing due to perceived low risk. Nearly all malaria-positive children received appropriate treatment in both arms (99.6% ePOCT + vs. 95.0% control). No significant difference was observed in inappropriate antimalarial prescriptions among malaria-negative or untested patients. Qualitative findings revealed barriers to testing, including rapid diagnostic test stockouts, staff shortages, low perceived local malaria risk, and caregiver refusal. Conclusions Implementation of ePOCT+ significantly increased malaria testing among febrile children, particularly in low-transmission settings, but did not change treatment practices, which were already largely appropriate. While CDSAs may standardize diagnostic practices and enhance adherence to testing guidelines, sustained impact requires addressing systemic constraints, including specific guidance and training for low-endemicity areas, improved supply chains, and sufficient human resources. Trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov identifier NCT05144763, 30.11.2021
